headline: ExxonMobil to operate Azerbaijan shale venture with SOCAR
summary_text: (Bloomberg) -- ExxonMobil has agreed to pump oil and natural gas from Azerbaijan’s shale fields as the Texas energy giant takes its fracing expertise overseas. ExxonMobil has entered a joint venture with Azerbaijan’s state oil company SOCAR that will allow it to explore and develop “unconventional hydrocarbon resources” in the Middle Kura basin, the companies said in a statement. ExxonMobil will operate the project, pending approval by the country’s legislature. U.S. shale has been the largest source of new global oil supplies for the past 15 years, transforming the country into the biggest producer of crude and exporter of liquefied natural gas. ExxonMobil and others are keen to take the lessons learned in the Permian basin and other U.S. shale fields to countries with similar geologic endowments. The legal and regulatory structures governing such drilling and oil production often are more complicated than in the U.S., requiring extensive negotiations before operations commence. ExxonMobil and SOCAR have been in talks for more than a year on the commercial and other aspects of the deal, which has been encouraged by the Trump administration. “We will combine SOCAR’s knowledge of Azerbaijan with ExxonMobil’s global experience and technology to better understand the basin’s potential and pursue opportunities for safe and efficient development,” said Bart Cahir, an ExxonMobil senior vice president.

headline: Exxon boasts of US$55B Guyana payday - Kaieteur News
summary_text: (Kaieteur News) – ExxonMobil has been able to recover an astounding US$55B it spent to develop the resources in Guyana, a remarkable achievement that the company now uses to advertise itself to countries that are looking for a similar achievement. During the Barclays Conference Fireside Chat on September 9, Exxon’s Senior Vice President and Chief Financial Officer (CFO), Neil Hansen discussed the milestone the company recently hit in Guyana where historic costs have been paid off. ... Exxon has invested in exploration and production activities in the Stabroek Block since 1999. While other countries do not allow oil companies to recover exploration costs, Guyana essentially pays Exxon to hunt for oil the Stabroek Block. Since 1999, costs have entered the ‘cost bank’ for exploration and subsequent development and operation of the projects. These were recovered or repaid using up to 75% of Guyana’s oil produced each month. Expenses not cleared in any given month are added to the following month’s expenditure until all costs are repaid. Up to the end of July 2026, Exxon revealed that all investments in the Stabroek Block have been recovered. ... of Guyana’ ... have often been criticized but ... During the recent Barclays event, Hansen said the projects in Guyana are well executed. “The desaturation of the cost bank was not a surprise. It did happen a lot faster than we expected, I think two years earlier, even when you adjust for the price impacts. So that is a reflection of, I think, the execution of the projects. It’s a reflection of operations and being able to run the existing FPSOs really well. And so, all of that accelerated the recovery of those costs, which is $55 billion,” he said. ... The Senior Vice President noted that Exxon will now receive about 100,000 barrels per day (bdp) less as a result of the earlier recovery of costs. Hansen however pointed out that the company is not finished in Guyana as plans are progressing for future developments. “We obviously continue to invest. We’ve got the fifth FPSO in the water today, in the waters of Guyana, so that’s progressing well. And we’re looking at advancing the ninth FPSO. So, again, it’s progressing well,” he shared. For Exxon, this demonstrates that the company is “the partner of choice”. Consequently, the Senior VP and CFO said, “If you’re a resource owner and you want someone to come in and execute a project like this in a way where the costs are recovered quickly and the investments recovered and the resource owner benefits from that more timely – ExxonMobil really is the partner of choice.” Moreover, he said the countries are now opting for one-on-one dialogues with oil companies instead of the “open bid type of approach” using Guyana as a prime example of what can be achieved. Last month President Irfaan Ali revealed that Guyana’s profit share has climbed significantly from 12.5% to 39.8% following the recovery of costs by Exxon. In accordance with the terms of the 2016 Production Sharing Agreement (PSA), Exxon was allowed to take up to 75% of the oil produced in Guyana each month until all of the company’s investments were repaid. The remaining 25% of oil each month is split between Guyana and the contractors, with the country receiving half of the “profit oil” or 12.5%. Stakeholders have called on government to ensure that the country’s current 39.8% profit share does not slide again to a meager 12.5% to finance more projects.

headline: Exxon Bids for Shell's $8 Billion U.S. Chemicals Business: Key Details | EpochEdge
summary_text: : Key Details Last updated: August 27, 2026 11:20 am David Brooks The chatter in lower Manhattan this morning isn’t just about the weather. Over on Pine Street, my phone has been buzzing non-stop since the Financial Times dropped its report. ExxonMobil, that bastion of American oil and gas, is circling Shell’s U.S. chemicals business. The price tag being whispered about? A cool eight billion dollars. Let’s be clear. This isn’t a rumor about some speculative startup. This is a potential tectonic shift in the industrial landscape, a move that could redraw the map for petrochemicals in North America. According to the FT’s unnamed sources, Exxon isn’t alone in the hunt. They’re up against heavyweight contenders like the plastics giant LyondellBasell, the private equity titan Apollo Global Management, and the state-backed Kuwait Petroleum Corporation. The fact that bids are already in, even if non-binding, tells you this process is moving with serious velocity. For Shell, this potential sale is the latest in a clear pattern. Just this month, they announced a deal to sell their European onshore wind and solar portfolio to TotalEnergies. Before that, it was a $720 million sale of a gas project stake offshore Cyprus to Hungary’s MOL. I covered Shell’s Capital Markets Day last year, where CEO Wael Sawan stood on that stage and promised a ruthless focus on “strongest long-term value.” He wasn’t kidding. They’re pruning assets that don’t fit the core mission, even profitable ones. That’s the disciplined, almost surgical, capital allocation Wall Street demands today. And make no mistake, Shell’s chemicals unit is profitable. Their Q2 earnings release showed adjusted earnings soaring to $9.84 billion, fueled in part by those very chemicals margins. The business in question—four major facilities across Louisiana, Texas, and Pennsylvania—is a workhorse. It produces the building blocks for everything from the plastic in your car to the detergent in your laundry. It’s a integrated, strategic asset. So why sell a crown jewel? The answer lies in the word “focus.” For Shell, the future is liquefied natural gas (LNG) and deep-water exploration. Chemicals, while lucrative, might be seen as a distraction from that singular ambition. For Exxon, however, chemicals are the future. Under CEO Darren Woods, Exxon has doubled down on its downstream and chemical operations, viewing them as a critical hedge against volatile oil prices and a growth engine in their own right. Acquiring Shell’s U.S. footprint would be a masterstroke of consolidation, giving Exxon even greater scale and market power in key regions like the Gulf Coast. ... - LyondellBasell looking for vertical integration - Apollo Global Management’s influence of private capital - Kuwait Petroleum’s national oil company strategy - Exxon’s focus on downstream and chemical operations - Shell’s emphasis on LNG and deep-water exploration - Regulatory scrutiny from the Federal Trade Commission The other bidders add fascinating layers. LyondellBasell would be looking for vertical integration, securing its own feedstock supply. Apollo Global Management represents the growing influence of private capital in energy infrastructure, seeing long-term value where public markets might be impatient. And Kuwait Petroleum? That’s a national oil company seeking a firmer foothold in the lucrative U.S. market, a strategic move that goes far beyond mere dollars and cents. The regulatory scrutiny here will be intense. A merger of Exxon and Shell’s chemical assets would create a behemoth with enormous pricing power. The Federal Trade Commission will have a field day. But in today’s environment, where scale is often seen as the only path to survival, the regulators might just have to swallow hard. I’ve walked the halls of these companies, interviewed their strategists, and listened to their earnings calls. This reported auction isn’t happening in a vacuum. It’s a direct consequence of the immense pressure these firms are under to deliver shareholder returns in a world demanding both energy security and an energy transition. Selling a strong business to fund a stronger ambition is the new calculus. As I file this from the Financial District, the only thing certain is uncertainty. But one thing is clear: the landscape of American industry is being reshaped, one multi-billion dollar deal at a time. headline: Borogue brings online new XLPE plant in UAE - Rubber World - The Technical Service Magazine for the Rubber Industry
summary_text: Vienna, Austria – Borouge Group International AG announced that, following the successful completion of performance testing, it has delivered the first batch of materials from its new Cross-Linked Polyethylene (XLPE) plant in the UAE to customers in the region. The new XLPE plant adds 100,000 tons of annual capacity, doubling Borouge International’s current XLPE output in the Middle East and Asia region per year. XLPE is used in high-voltage underground and underwater power cables that support grid expansion, electrification, and the transformation of energy systems. Borouge Plc, part of Borouge International, operates the region’s only XLPE plant of its kind, strengthening its ability to meet rising demand from fast-growing economies and data centers across Asia and the Middle East. Borouge International collaborated with Ducab, a leading UAE-based end-to-end energy solutions provider and manufacturer of high-quality cables and wires, to successfully test the performance of the initial batch of materials produced at the new XLPE plant. Following the successful completion of testing, Borouge International is ramping up production at the new plant to deliver material for medium and high voltage applications that will support the global energy transformation and decarbonization initiatives. Hazeem Sultan Al Suwaidi, Chief Executive Officer of Borouge Plc and Chairman of Borouge 4, said: “The first customer deliveries from our new XLPE plant mark an important milestone in the Borouge 4 growth journey and demonstrate our ability to bring advanced production capacity to meet evolving market demand. By expanding our XLPE production capabilities, we are strengthening our position in high-value energy applications, supporting critical grid and network developments in the UAE and beyond, while continuing to deliver sustainable long-term value for our shareholders.” As part of the required approval process for any materials produced at the new XLPE facility, Borouge International completed extensive benchmark testing against approved materials from its existing assets. Building on the ongoing collaboration between Borouge International and Ducab, medium and high voltage cables will be manufactured at Ducab’s cable plant where they have been subjected to a rigorous testing program in accordance with international standards. ... Borouge International and Ducab’s collaboration has supported landmark UAE developments including Saadiyat Cultural District, Zayed National Museum, Ducab Headquarters, and the Borouge 4 expansion, with future demand expected from major projects such as Palm Jebel Ali. Borouge 4 will be operated by Borouge Plc on behalf of the project’s owners ADNOC and OMV and will boost the company’s production capacity by 1.4 million tonnes to make Ruwais the world’s largest single-site polyolefin complex. Borouge 4 is expected to generate a cumulative net profit of up to $400 million over three years, representing approximately 10% annual accretion to Borouge Plc earnings post-ramp-up. Borouge Plc has been granted operational control and marketing rights for Borouge 4 by the project owners via a usage agreement. This framework gives Borouge Plc greater flexibility in managing the asset and in capturing value over time, without requiring upfront capital investment from Borouge Plc.

headline: UAE Petrochemical Hub Restarts: Borouge Restores Ruwais Output After April Attack — SupplyStatus
summary_text: Borouge Plc has restored full production availability at its Ruwais complex in the United Arab Emirates after asset damage caused by the regional conflict on 5 April 2026, but the site is still running well below normal rates. The company confirmed on 31 July 2026 that repairs were completed by the end of June, ahead of its own schedule, and that it now plans a return to high utilization during the second half of the year. That recovery depends on two things the company does not control: feedstock supply and shipping conditions in the Gulf. The damage happened on 5 April 2026, when falling debris from an intercepted aerial attack hit production units in the Ruwais Industrial Area. Borouge told the Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange on 6 April that air defences had intercepted the incoming threat, that the resulting fires were brought under control and that no one was injured. Production in the affected areas was suspended while damage was assessed. The strikes were part of the wider conflict between Iran and the United States and Israel that began on 28 February 2026 and closed the Strait of Hormuz to most commercial traffic. The cost of that shutdown is visible in the numbers. Borouge produced 721,000 tonnes in the second quarter, roughly 24 percent less than in the same quarter of 2025, a period that had itself been reduced by a major planned turnaround. Utilization averaged 60 percent across the complex, split between 48 percent for polyethylene and 71 percent for polypropylene. Sales volumes reached 873,000 tonnes, above production, because the company drew down 98,000 tonnes of inventory built in the first quarter and pulled in 54,000 tonnes from other sources inside the group. The logistics response is the part of the story that matters most for buyers. Borouge activated contingency plans in March 2026 and built export routes by road, rail and sea that avoid the Strait of Hormuz entirely. Management confirmed at the end of July that all volumes are now shipped without using the waterway, moving cargo through the country's east coast. Asia-Pacific took 49 percent of second quarter sales and the Middle East and Africa took 41 percent, up two points on the previous quarter as land freight expanded. The workaround came at a price, with selling and distribution costs rising to 254 dollars per tonne. Higher prices covered much of the damage. Revenue rose 20 percent quarter on quarter to 1.4 billion dollars and net profit rose 23 percent to 191 million dollars, helped by a 53 percent jump in average realised prices and by about 25 million dollars of insurance proceeds. Adjusted EBITDA of 401 million dollars was 9 percent lower than a year earlier, with the margin at 29 percent, five points below the 2025 level, because of higher propylene feedstock costs and freight. Net debt reached 3.3 billion dollars at the end of June, up from 2.7 billion at the end of 2025. Repair costs are expected to keep 2026 maintenance spending below 300 million dollars. As of early August 2026 the complex is running between 60 and 70 percent utilization, the level reported through July, with daily swings above that range. Feedstock availability, not export capacity, is the binding constraint. The Strait of Hormuz remains effectively closed to normal commercial traffic after a June memorandum between Washington and Tehran broke down in July, so the propylene and other feed supplies the plants depend on stay tight. Prices are expected to ease from here. Borouge told investors that third quarter polyolefin prices should moderate from the very strong second quarter level while staying above historical averages, as operating rates recover across Asia and regional supply constraints ease. Benchmark prices already softened in July, and propylene feedstock costs have come down from their peak although they remain above pre-conflict levels. The record prices were described as temporary and are expected to normalize over time. The wider polyolefin market explains why these prices were so high. Borouge estimates that around 29 million tonnes of polyethylene and polypropylene capacity in its core Asia-Pacific markets, close to 19 percent of the regional total, was affected by Middle East feedstock shortages during the quarter. Many plants ran below normal rates for much of the period. That shortage lifted global prices to record or near record levels in April and May before balances started to normalize in June. For buyers, the practical question in the second half is whether Ruwais volumes return before prices fall further. Borouge has set out two scenarios. If the Strait of Hormuz reopens in a durable way, polyolefin prices should normalize while utilization rises and feedstock and freight costs fall. If restrictions continue, prices stay elevated but the complex may not be able to lift output much beyond current levels. The first units of the Borouge 4 expansion are also arriving, with a second cross-linked polyethylene plant now in commercial production and adding 100,000 tonnes a year, and further units due to start during the rest of 2026 and in 2027. ... headline: IOCL BPCL HPCL Q2 Earnings: IOCL, BPCL, HPCL likely to see Q2 earnings recovery but crude supply shock, tariff risk may play spoilsport, ETEnergyworld
summary_text: India's state-run oil marketing companies, IOCL, BPCL, and HPCL, are on track for a upbeat Q2 financial recovery driven by robust diesel margins and crude inventory gains, JM Financial highlights. ... M Financial projects Q2 FY27 EBITDA to bounce back to ₹10,700 crore for IOCL and ₹8,000 crore for BPCL. While Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd (HPCL) is still expected to report a loss. India’s top oil refiners such as Indian Oil Corporation Ltd (IOCL), Bharat Petroleum Corporation Ltd (BPCL) and others are bracing for a much-needed financial rebound in the second quarter, but a storm of global supply disruptions and looming US trade tariffs threatens to spoil the party. According to a recent sector update by JM Financial, India's state-run oil marketing companies are eyeing a quarter-on-quarter earnings recovery, even as a complex web of geopolitical risks keeps the broader outlook deeply uncertain. Refining a recovery The financial pain that battered the sector in the first quarter is expected to ease significantly. JM Financial projects Q2 FY27 EBITDA to bounce back to ₹10,700 crore for IOCL and ₹8,000 crore for BPCL. While Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd (HPCL) is still expected to report a loss, the deficit is projected to narrow drastically to a negative ₹2,700 crore. This revival is heavily anchored on "strong diesel crack-led reported GRMs of $32-40/bbl," the brokerage said. The brokerage report attributed the turnaround to crude inventory gains, projecting $3 per barrel for IOCL and $2 per barrel each for BPCL and HPCL. Furthermore, a welcome dip in global LPG prices is expected to slash under-recoveries to roughly ₹11,000 crore, or ₹250 per cylinder, down from a punishing ₹21,200 crore in the previous quarter. The bleeding at the retail pumps is also expected to slow down, with auto-fuel marketing losses shrinking to a negative ₹17.5 per litre, aided by a full-quarter impact of earlier petrol and diesel price hikes. Oil on a boil However, another report from JM Financial warns that crude supply shocks could quickly pressure these margins. Spot Brent prices recently skyrocketed to $125 per barrel, driven by near-term crude availability tightness. Houthi attacks have battered Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, choking off approximately 4.5 million barrels per day of crude exports via the Red Sea. If these disruptions persist, the Middle East oil export shortfall could balloon to 10-12 million barrels per day. The International Energy Agency (IEA) anticipates a global oil market deficit of 1.7 million barrels per day in CY26, prompting analysts to caution that Iran seems intent on "keeping oil on a boil" to influence upcoming US mid-term elections, JM Financial report noted. US tariffs Adding another layer of complexity, a third JM Financial strategy report highlighted that India is increasingly finding itself in the crosshairs of aggressive US trade policies. The newly enacted Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act grants the US administration the authority to slap tariffs of up to 100 per cent on goods imported from nations making major Russian energy purchases. Russia supplied a massive 44.7 per cent of India's crude oil imports in the year-to-date period for FY27, pushing the total crude import bill to $63.3 billion through July 2026. While the Ministry of External Affairs has maintained its commitment to energy security for its 1.4 billion citizens through "diversified sourcing and evolving market dynamics", the tariff risk is palpable, it said.

headline: HPCL-led energy fund to back deep-tech start-ups; targets to cut industry’s refining bill worth ₹1 lakh crore - The Hindu
summary_text: A band of public sector oil and gas companies, led by Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd. (HPCL), is setting up a deep-tech incubation and investment ecosystem aimed at solving some of the energy sector’s biggest technology challenges, including an opportunity to cut the nearly ₹1 lakh crore that India’s refining industry spends annually on energy, said HPCL Chairman and Managing Director Vikas Kaushal here on Tuesday. A consortium of oil companies have formed a Section 8 company, MC2 Plus, which would operate as an incubator and accelerator for start-ups working on deep technology for the core energy sector. The initiative would subsequently be backed by a professionally managed Alternative Investment Fund (AIF), which Mr. Kaushal described as an “India Energy Fund,” with a sizeable corpus for investing in energy-focused start-ups. The proposed fund is expected to be launched shortly, he added. ... According to Mr. Kaushal, the scale of the opportunity is particularly significant in refining. India has around 270 million tones of refining capacity, and the sector spends close to ₹1 lakh crore a year on energy used in the refining process alone. The figure does not include the energy required for transporting and distributing petroleum products. He argued that the changing energy landscape was making these challenges increasingly complex. Refiners now have multiple options for sourcing electricity and fuels, including grid power, captive generation and renewable electricity, besides conventional fuels such as gas, naphtha and fuel oil. At the same time, crude and fuel prices have become more volatile, while new fuels and technologies such as green hydrogen, energy storage and round-the-clock renewable power were emerging, he added. This convergence, Mr. Kaushal, created a large number of technology problems that could become opportunities for start-ups. “You have ₹1 lakh crore of money being spent. You have these many new options which are coming up,” he said urging entrepreneurs and researchers in the audience to find ways of optimising energy consumption and costs in the sector. ... According to Mr. Kaushal said India’s start-up ecosystem had expanded rapidly, with more than 1.15 lakh startups registered with the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade and the country already has 130 unicorns. However, much of the innovation in the energy sector has been concentrated in newer segments rather than the core energy industry. Of the more than 13,000 energy-related start-ups in the country, nearly 45% were working in electric vehicles and mobility, according to data cited by Mr. Kaushal. Battery storage, solar energy and hydrogen have also emerged as important areas of start-up activity. The gap, he said, was deep technology aimed at improving the efficiency and economics of the existing energy system. Five of India’s top 10 companies by turnover are core energy companies or have significant energy operations, highlighting the economic importance of the sector, he said. “Deep-tech, as I would call in the core energy, is something which we missed significantly in the last decade,” Mr. Kaushal said. ... The oil and gas sector itself has been slow to tap the start-up ecosystem, he acknowledged. For instance, HPCL had invested around ₹30 crore in startups over the past six to seven years when it could actually had the ability to invest ₹3,000 crore in that same period and that was a miss the sector had,’’ he lamented. MC2 Plus was intended to address this gap by pooling the capabilities of several oil and gas companies rather than having individual companies pursue start-ups independently. HPCL would establish an incubator at its research facility in Bengaluru, Mr. Kaushal said, while other oil-sector companies are also expected to open their research infrastructure to start-ups. Mr. Kaushal said the platform would seek participation from start-ups, students, researchers and academics and urged entrepreneurs to approach the programme with solutions to real-world energy problems. “We want to create a deep-tech ecosystem in the country in the core energy domain,” he said.

headline: HPCL eyes LNG supply diversification beyond Middle East; plans Rs 5,000 crore gas investment in 3-5 years: ED Natural Gas Anuj Mehrotra
summary_text: HPCL eyes ... diversification beyond Middle ... ; plans Rs 5,000 crore gas investment in 3-5 years: ... Natural Gas Anuj Mehrotra ... State-run Hindustan Petroleum Corp is evaluating gas purchases from North America, Africa, and Australia to reduce its dependence on the Middle East and diversify supply base as the West Asia conflict continues to disrupt gas supplies, the company’s executive director, natural gas Anuj Mehrotra told Moneycontrol in an interview. HPCL will evaluate opportunities across the energy value chain, including potential upstream gas assets in India or overseas. ... HPCL sources 47 percent of its LNG from the Middle East which has been disrupted due to the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. ... State-run Hindustan Petroleum Corp (HPCL) is evaluating liquefied natural gas (LNG) sourcing opportunities from North America, Africa and Australia as it seeks to reduce its dependence on the Middle East and diversify its gas supply base amid continued disruptions in West Asia. The company currently sources 47 percent of its LNG from the Middle East, while Qatar is its largest supplier. HPCL Executive Director, Natural Gas Anuj Mehrotra told Moneycontrol that recent developments in the region have reinforced the need for a more diversified and flexible procurement strategy. “Going forward, diversification will be a deliberate part of our procurement strategy. We will look at sourcing opportunities from geographies such as North America, Africa, and Australia, among others, to reduce regional concentration risk. We will also continue to leverage Chhara, greenfield liquefied natural gas storage and regasification facility located in Gujarat, developed and explore additional domestic gas opportunities wherever feasible,” Mehrotra said. HPCL’s LNG portfolio combines long-term contracts with spot procurement, while the company is also exploring domestic gas opportunities. “We also see Compressed Biogas (CBG) and other renewable gases as complementary sources of energy. So, our objective is not simply to secure more LNG, but to build a resilient portfolio combining long-term LNG, spot procurement, multiple sourcing geographies, domestic gas and renewable gas,” he said. India imports nearly 60 percent of its total LNG from the Middle East, with Qatar accounting for 47 percent. The company’s diversification plans come as the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz has disrupted gas supplies from the region. ... HPCL has lined up an investment of Rs 5,000 crore across the natural gas value chain over the next three to five years. Around 70-80 percent of the planned investment will be directed towards city gas distribution (CGD) expansion, including strengthening steel and Medium-Density Polyethylene (MDPE) networks, adding CNG and city gas stations, expanding domestic piped natural gas (PNG) and growing industrial and commercial PNG, Mehrotra said. Around 20 percent of the investment will support LNG infrastructure, including the Chhara LNG ecosystem and LNG mobility. The remaining funds will be directed towards CBG, digitalisation, smart metering and other emerging opportunities. HPCL has already commissioned two CBG plants and plans to commission another 24 over the next five years. The company has also entered into agreements with more than 12 existing and upcoming CBG producers since 2023 for procurement of the fuel. HPCL achieved around 1.7 percent CBG blending during FY26 and is targeting 3 percent blending in FY27. “The CBG will be integrated into our CGD network and supplied through our existing infrastructure to CNG, D-PNG and Industrial & Commercial customers,” Mehrotra said. This deployment aims to support long-term refining asset optimization and value creation across the multi-unit complex. High-Yield Bottom-of-the-Barrel Conversion The custom engineering of the high-yield ROSE solvent deasphalting unit allows the residue upgradation facility to extract higher-value petroleum products from low-value, bottom-of-the-barrel streams. The physical separation plant is configured to process and convert approximately 93 percent of the heavy residue feedstocks. This high conversion efficiency is projected to expand the absolute distillate yields at the Visakh refinery while increasing baseline gross refining margins. Functioning as a core component of India’s first commercial residue hydrocracking unit, the project establishes a landmark reference for the technical integration of supercritical fluid extraction technologies. Gary Godwin, Vice President of Energy Products and Services at KBR, stated that the repeat selection reflects the long-term performance and field reliability of the technology. Godwin noted that the organization remains focused on advancing refining and clean fuels solutions to match evolving global market criteria while adapting to the unique requirements of next-generation refinery architectures. The vendor maintains a greater than 90 percent market share within the supercritical solvent deasphalting sector, with a global combined licensed capacity approaching 1.8 million barrels per stream day across a customer network that includes numerous repeat licensees. The underlying process is continuously enhanced, providing multiple distinct process flow schemes to support optimal integration with both grassroots installations and pre-existing brownfield facilities. Additional Context This section details technical specifications not included in the original news release. The Residuum Oil Supercritical Extraction (ROSE) process is an advanced, energy-efficient variation of solvent deasphalting (SDA) that relies on the thermodynamic behavior of solvents near or above their critical temperature and pressure thresholds. In conventional solvent deasphalting, heavy vacuum residuum feedstocks are mixed with light hydrocarbon solvents—typically propane, butane, or pentane—to separate paraffinic deasphalted oil (DAO) from heavy, highly aromatic asphaltene fractions based on solubility deltas. Traditional plants require vast amounts of thermal energy to distill and vaporize the solvent away from the extracted oil phase, followed by intensive cooling to condense the solvent back into a liquid state for reuse. The supercritical process eliminates this energy-intensive phase-change loop by operating the solvent recovery section above the solvent's specific critical point. At supercritical conditions, the liquid and gas phases of the fluid become indistinguishable, and the solvent's density and solvating power drop sharply with minor temperature adjustments. Inside the ROSE separator vessel, the temperature of the solvent-DAO mixture is elevated slightly above the critical threshold; the solvent loses its ability to hold the oil in solution, causing the deasphalted oil to precipitate out as a distinct liquid phase. The near-density solvent can then be drawn off from the top of the vessel and recycled directly back to the primary extractor as a dense fluid without passing through a latent heat of vaporization or condensation cycle. This reduces utility steam consumption and cooling water loads by up to 60% compared to traditional evaporation-based separation units, optimizing process efficiency within high-capacity residue hydrocracking configurations. State-run Hindustan Petroleum Corporation’s (HPCL) company-wide EBITDA improvement programme, Project Samridhi aided the oil marketing company (OMC) in increasing earnings by $0.54 per barrel across its entire marketing volume, or roughly ₹1,691 crore. HPCL had set a target of improving EBITDA by $0.50 per barrel across its sales volume for the last financial year. Launched in May 2025 to counter sustained cost and margin pressures faced by the refining and marketing business, Project Samridhi was conceived to move beyond isolated, one-time cost-saving measures and establish a permanent, governance-led framework for identifying and capturing value across the organisation. ... on three key pillars — ... reduction and structural process transformation. ... The total EBITDA improvement comprised ₹ 744 crore in recurring benefits and ₹ 947 crore in one-time benefits. In refinery operations, the programme delivered savings of ₹ 428 per tonne of crude throughput across 26.04 mt processed, equivalent to $0.66 per barrel. In the marketing business, savings of ₹ 119 per tonne of sales volume across 48.53 mt sold translated into an impact of $0.18 per barrel. Besides, the cost-take-out initiatives contributed ₹288 crore, while the margin improvements initiatives delivered ₹1,403 crore. Contribution from margin improvement items was majorly delivered through a combination of various initiatives such as crude value maximisation, refinery efficiency improvements, supply optimisation, logistics efficiencies, and strategic commercial interventions. ... “In an industry where profitability is often shaped by factors beyond a company’s control, right from geopolitical developments and crude oil price fluctuations to refining spreads and logistics costs, operational excellence has become a critical differentiator, Vinod stressed. Against this backdrop, Project Samridhi is emerging as a significant example of how HPCL can create value through internal transformation. The project is built around the philosophy of structural cost takeout and efficiency improvement, which involves the strategic reduction of fixed costs deeply embedded within operations, independent of business volumes, he added.

headline: Westrock Coffee’s $360m investment now a “generator of cash”, says CEO
summary_text: The US beverage manufacturer says its three-year investment programme is beginning to deliver, with new RTD and single-serve capacity supporting revenue growth, narrowing losses and a stronger pipeline of brand partners Westrock Coffee has moved into the next phase of its growth plan, reporting its fifth consecutive quarter of year-on-year improvement in adjusted EBITDA and generating positive free cash flow earlier than expected. The Arkansas-based coffee roaster, packager and supplier posted second-quarter net sales of $305.7m, up 8.8% from the same period last year. Its net loss narrowed to $13.7m from $21.6m compared to a year ago, while its operating loss fell to $1.4m from $15m. Adjusted EBITDA, Westrock’s preferred measure of underlying profitability, rose 38.9% to $21.3m. Chief Financial Officer Chris Pledger said the figures showed “continued momentum across our platform”. He added that Beverage Solutions sales rose 16.8% to $243.9m, with adjusted EBITDA up 12.7% to $22.2m. Gross profit fell 8.8% to $37.7m, however, as depreciation from the Conway assets and non-cash adjustments weighed on the quarter. ... Westrock invested approximately $360m in new RTD and single-serve facilities, including its 524,000-square-foot Conway, Arkansas site, which it describes as the world’s largest roast-to-RTD manufacturing facility. “The platform we spent the last three years building no longer requires capital. Rather, it is a generator of cash,” said CEO and co-founder Scott Ford. Westrock generated $20.2m in free cash flow during the quarter and was cash-flow positive for the first half of the year, one quarter ahead of its previous schedule. Conway is now contributing across multiple beverage channels. Ford said Beverage Solutions growth was led by higher volumes of RTD cans, glass bottles and multi-serve formats, with demand coming from both existing and new brand partners. The company is also supplying packaged coffee and single-serve cups, while expanding into adjacent categories. Pledger said growth was supported by “new customer wins in our flavours, extracts, and ingredients business, including the launch of a lemonade refreshers program”. Ford said the pipeline now includes refreshers, energy and high-protein drinks, as well as functional and nutraceutical single-serve cups. Single-serve coffee volumes increased 9% year-on-year when excluding a customer lost through industry consolidation. Ford said Westrock is growing at roughly four times the rate of the overall single-serve cup market, with replacement volumes from new customers expected to begin arriving late this year and build through 2027. The company says its expanded capacity is helping it win business across multiple product lines. “We are across the board winning share in every single category that we play in,” Ford told investors. He said customers are initially approaching Westrock for one product, then expanding their relationship after seeing the company’s manufacturing, sourcing and risk-management capabilities. Notably, in July Westrock Coffee struck a major ready-to-drink partnership with Italian coffee illycaffè for the US market. Westrock expects further growth without another major construction project. Ford said recent can-format wins should make Conway an increasingly important contributor to profitability through the rest of 2026 and into next year. The company is also developing four new format lines this year and has eight products in development that it expects to launch over the next 24 months, provided they are supported by committed customer demand. With its heavy investment phase largely complete, Westrock reaffirmed its 2026 adjusted EBITDA outlook of $90m to $100m. Pledger said the company’s priorities are now to sell remaining capacity, manage its customer mix and improve operations across its plants. Ford said the business is “on the precipice of becoming a very, very different business than the one that we have been”. The next test will be turning the Conway platform’s growing sales pipeline into sustained profit growth, while using cash generation to reduce debt rather than begin another costly expansion cycle.

To understand the significance of today’s financial news, one must first appreciate the sheer scale of the Conway project. Since 2021, Westrock has poured over $300 million into transforming a 524,000-square-foot facility into what is now the largest of its kind in the United States. This wasn't just an expansion; it was a fundamental reinvention of the company’s operational core, designed to shift its focus from traditional coffee roasting toward the higher-margin, high-growth world of ready-to-drink (RTD) beverages, extracts, and complex ingredients. The term “peak investment phase” is a stark understatement. Company filings show capital expenditures ballooning to approximately $160 million in 2024 as the facility was built out. That number fell to $89 million in 2025, and by the first quarter of 2026, it had plummeted to just $7 million. This dramatic drop is the clearest evidence that the heavy lifting is done. The massive capital sink that was Conway is now a fully commercialized, cash-flow-positive asset. With all five of its advanced production lines now operational, the facility that once consumed capital is now primed to generate it. This operational milestone is the direct enabler of the financial restructuring. The company’s lenders, a syndicate that now includes Texas Capital Bank, are not extending terms out of charity; they are responding to a fundamentally de-risked business profile. The proven performance of the Conway plant, which has effectively doubled Westrock's operational footprint, provides the confidence needed to offer more favorable terms. ... The details of the amended credit agreement read like a report card of a company that has earned its lenders' trust. By exiting the covenant relief period early, Westrock has voluntarily accepted a tighter leash. The maximum permitted secured net leverage ratio, a key measure of debt relative to earnings, will now be capped at 4.00x, down from a temporary ceiling of 5.00x. In corporate finance, offering to abide by stricter rules is a power move. It signals profound confidence from management that future earnings will comfortably support the debt load. The reward for this confidence is immediate and tangible: lower borrowing costs. The early termination triggers a decrease in the applicable interest margin on its loans, which will directly reduce interest expenses and bolster the bottom line. According to one credit analyst, this move effectively trades temporary covenant flexibility for longer-term stability and lower costs—a trade any healthy, growing company would make. This confidence is backed by tangible results. After a rocky period post-SPAC, Westrock's performance is showing a sharp upward trajectory. In the first quarter of 2026, the company more than tripled its consolidated adjusted EBITDA year-over-year to $26 million and swung from a $13.1 million operating loss to a $3.2 million operating income. Its secured net leverage ratio had already improved to 3.45x, well within the new, stricter covenant. The company isn’t just hoping for future performance; it’s already delivering it. ... This newfound financial flexibility isn't an end in itself; it's fuel for Westrock's strategic ambitions. The company is positioning itself as the essential behind-the-scenes partner for the world's largest brands, capitalizing on the biggest trends shaping the $5 trillion global beverage market. The “cold coffee revolution,” the explosive growth in functional beverages promising everything from energy to focus, and the unwavering consumer demand for convenience are all squarely in Conway’s wheelhouse. The plant's capabilities in canning, bottling, and producing complex extracts allow Westrock to move beyond being a private-label supplier and become an integrated solutions platform. It is already developing high-protein beverages for leading CPG brands and expanding its capabilities for milk-based RTD products and energy drinks. This aligns perfectly with a market where RTD beverages are projected to grow from $732 billion to over $1.2 trillion by 2032. Furthermore, this operational and financial stability reinforces the company's competitive advantage in sustainability. Westrock recently announced it had achieved 100% responsibly sourced green coffee and tea purchases, a powerful differentiator in a market of increasingly conscious consumers. Financial strength allows the company to maintain and expand these ethical sourcing programs, which are not just good for the world but are also good for business, attracting premium partners who value a transparent and traceable supply chain. ... For investors who have watched Westrock since its public debut, this moment feels like a turning point. The narrative is shifting from one of potential and investment to one of execution and monetization. The company has successfully navigated the most difficult and capital-intensive part of its transformation. The operational engine in Conway is running, the financial structure has been fortified, and the market trends are blowing squarely at its back. The road ahead will require continued discipline. Management has acknowledged the loss of a large single-serve customer due to M&A activity but projects it will backfill that capacity by 2027, driven by a strong sales pipeline for the new capabilities at Conway. Today’s announcement demonstrates that Westrock has secured the financial stability and runway necessary to see that strategy through. The focus now shifts from building the factory to filling it, proving that the massive bet on Conway can deliver the sustained profitability and growth the company has long promised.

headline: US coalition files trade petition over corrugated pizza box imports
summary_text: The American Pizza Boxes Manufacturers Coalition has filed a petition seeking antidumping duties on imports of corrugated pizza boxes from China, Malaysia and Türkiye. The coalition, comprising Smurfit Westrock and Pratt Industries, filed the petition on September 9 alongside the United Steel, Paper and Forestry, Rubber, Manufacturing, Energy, Allied Industrial and Service Workers International Union (USW) . The petitioners are also seeking countervailing duties on imports from Türkiye. The proposed investigation covers corrugated food service boxes commonly used for pizzas, including finished boxes and die-cut blanks supplied flat for assembly. Products manufactured from B-, C-, D- and E-flute corrugated board, as well as equivalent flute types, are included within the proposed scope.

The group calls itself the American Pizza Boxes Manufacturers Coalition and is composed of Smurfit Westrock and Pratt Industries, according to a news release from Wiley Rein, the law firm representing the coalition. The United Steelworkers union also jointly filed the petitions. Next, Commerce is expected to determine within 20 days whether to initiate investigations, and the USITC is expected to issue a preliminary determination within 45 days, the law firm said.

headline: ReposiTrak’s Touchless Retail™ Begins Deployment for Leading Paper Goods Supplier with Large Eastern Retailer
summary_text: # ReposiTrak’s Touchless Retail™ Begins Deployment for Leading Paper Goods Supplier with Large Eastern Retailer ... # ReposiTrak’s Touchless Retail™ Begins Deployment for Leading Paper Goods Supplier with Large Eastern Retailer By: ReposiTrak, Inc. via Business Wire September 17, 2026 at 07:00 AM EDT Supplier Adoption Accelerates as Touchless Retail™ Moves Rapidly from Launch to Deployment ReposiTrak, Inc. (NYSE: TRAK), the leader in retail supply chain, merchandising, compliance and traceability solutions, today announced that implementation of Touchless Retail™ is underway with a paper products supplier at a large East Coast retailer. Touchless Retail combines ReposiTrak’s best-in-class DSD technology, including perpetual inventory, demand-driven ordering and out-of-stock visibility—with an elite merchandising team made up of the top 10% of merchandisers. The result is smarter, more consistent shelf execution at a fixed, predictable cost that is typically 50% lower than traditional hourly merchandising. The retailer is also evaluating broader deployment of Touchless Retail to improve in-stock performance and reduce out-of-stocks across its DSD supplier base. The combination of advanced technology, top-tier execution and significantly lower, predictable costs is driving strong market interest in Touchless Retail. “Touchless Retail is moving from market introduction to implementation,” said Randy Fields, chairman and CEO of ReposiTrak. “Our first supplier contracts have been signed, and deployment is underway. Paper products are an excellent example of a category where shelf availability, presentation and consistent execution matter. Suppliers need a better way to manage that work without accepting unpredictable merchandising costs or inconsistent results.” Touchless Retail has been extremely well received across categories and addresses two persistent problems for direct store delivery (DSD) suppliers managing products at retail: - High and unpredictable merchandising costs, including variable hourly rates, travel charges and other expenses that make programs difficult to budget and scale - Inconsistent store-level execution, with limited visibility into who performed the work, what was completed and whether products were properly stocked, displayed and represented at the shelf For paper products suppliers, those challenges can directly affect product availability, shelf presentation and sales. Large, high-volume products require consistent attention to inventory conditions, shelf replenishment and merchandising execution to help keep products available and properly presented to shoppers. Touchless Retail replaces traditional merchandising uncertainty with a fixed cost that is typically about 50% less than traditional merchandising models and store-level execution by an APEX Certified Team composed of SPAR’s elite merchandisers. The solution is delivered through the relationship between ReposiTrak and SPAR Group, Inc. (OTCQB: SGRP). ReposiTrak manages the integrated Touchless Retail program, including technology, data, supplier onboarding and operational coordination. SPAR provides the experienced field organization responsible for in-store execution. SPAR has more than 55 years of merchandising experience and a nationwide network of more than 6,000 merchandisers. For Touchless Retail programs, only the top-performing 10% of that network qualifies for the elite APEX team. These proven merchandisers deliver exceptional execution, with an on time visit rate exceeding 99.5% and a revisit rate of less than 0.5%. “This is not simply access to merchandising labor,” Fields added. “Before deployment begins, we establish the stores, products, service requirements and execution standards. For a paper products supplier, that means having a disciplined approach to keeping the right products properly represented at the shelf. The supplier knows what the program will cost, who is representing its brand and how execution will be managed.” Touchless Retail is available to suppliers across all categories delivered by DSD. “Traditional merchandising has forced suppliers to accept unpredictable costs without always knowing who is representing their brand or whether the work was completed to their standards,” said William Linanne, CEO of SPAR Group. “By combining ReposiTrak’s technology and data capabilities with SPAR’s professional merchandising organization, Touchless Retail changes that equation. Suppliers can gain predictable costs, stronger store-level execution and greater confidence that their products are available and properly represented at the shelf.” With the paper products supplier implementation underway, Touchless Retail is advancing a new merchandising model built around lower costs, higher-quality execution and measurable accountability. headline: International Paper Finishes $250M Riverdale Conversion — But Its New Containerboard Capacity Is Still Undisclosed - corruga.expert
summary_text: International Paper has completed the $250 million conversion of paper machine No. 16 at its Riverdale Mill in Selma, Alabama, from uncoated freesheet to containerboard — but the company has not disclosed PM16’s new annual containerboard capacity. For corrugated board producers, that missing number changes how the story should be read: this is not yet a simple “new tons entering the market” story. It is a test of whether International Paper can turn an existing machine into qualified, lower-cost, higher-value packaging supply and then use its integrated mill-and-box network to make those tons more competitive. The conversion is complete, but the commercial impact is only starting. International Paper says the ramp should be largely achieved by the end of 2026, with full run rate expected in Q1 2027. That means the next two quarters — customer qualification, grade mix, operating stability and where the paper is deployed — may matter more to the corrugated market than the $250 million headline itself. ... the combined announced investment in Riverdale’s two major machine conversions: roughly $300 million for PM15 beginning in 2017 and $250 million for PM16. ... International Paper has been explicit about the strategy behind Riverdale: the investment is intended to strengthen product mix, improve its cost position and support more lightweight and high-performance packaging grades for strategic customers. ... On International Paper’s Q2 2026 earnings call, Chairman and CEO Andrew Silvernail said: “The machine conversion is complete and the ramp up is progressing as expected.” Management expects the ramp to be largely achieved by year-end 2026 and full run rate in the first quarter of 2027. The ramp period is also being used to qualify the machine with customers across product lines. ... International Paper also said the four major investments highlighted on its Q2 call — including Riverdale — are expected to generate financial returns in the mid-teens to mid-20s. The company did not provide a standalone ROI for PM16, so that broader investment range should not be presented as a Riverdale-specific return target. ... PM16 is not the first major grade shift at Riverdale. In 2017, International Paper announced an approximately $300 million conversion of PM15 from uncoated freesheet to high-quality whitetop linerboard and containerboard. At the time, the company said PM15 would add 450,000 tons of annual containerboard capacity and give the mill greater product flexibility. Now PM16 has followed with another $250 million investment. Together, the two projects represent roughly $550 million of announced conversion capital at the same Alabama mill in less than a decade. That is more revealing than treating PM16 as an isolated project. International Paper has repeatedly chosen to put major capital into Riverdale rather than abandon the site or replace it with a greenfield mill. The company is taking an existing industrial platform — fibre supply, energy, labour, maintenance, rail and truck logistics — and changing what that platform produces for the packaging market. ... Later in the Q2 call, Silvernail described International Paper’s North American strategy in unusually clear terms: the company wants to be the low-cost player, not the low-price player, and is integrating its mill and box networks more tightly so the right paper is made in the right locations and delivered with lower cost and better service. ... The immediate risk is not necessarily a sudden wave of extra containerboard. International Paper has not disclosed enough data to make that claim. The more important pressure could come from product mix and delivered economics. If Riverdale successfully qualifies more lightweight and high-performance grades, International Paper can combine paper production with its converting network and compete on the total economics of the package — paper performance, box design, logistics, reliability and service — rather than only on the price of a box. That is especially relevant because International Paper itself describes corrugated packaging competition as highly local: most competition happens within roughly 250 miles of a customer facility. A lower-cost paper position at the mill level can therefore become a very local competitive advantage when it feeds the right box plants in the right markets. ... Before the conversion, Riverdale supplied Sylvamo with cutsize uncoated freesheet under an agreement linked to the companies’ 2021 separation. Sylvamo expected about 260,000 short tons from Riverdale in 2025 and around 100,000 short tons in 2026 before the agreement ended. As that supply disappeared, Sylvamo had to rebuild its North American sourcing plan using inventory, third-party conversion and imports from its own mills. Management said changes in U.S. tariff rates led it to bring more product from Brazil while reducing planned European imports. At the same time, Sylvamo is investing $145 million at its Eastover mill in South Carolina. Its program includes a paper-machine optimization expected to add around 60,000 short tons of annual uncoated freesheet capacity and a new cutsize sheeter with 100,000 short tons of additional sheeting capability. The direct effect here is on the uncoated freesheet market, not proof of a global containerboard shortage or surplus. But the chain reaction is important: one machine changes grade in Alabama, a former customer changes transatlantic sourcing, Brazilian and European flows move, another U.S. mill receives new capital, and International Paper redirects the original asset into containerboard. ... PM16 ramps on schedule, the intended grades qualify quickly and International Paper enters 2027 with a stronger Riverdale cost position and more lightweight and high-performance supply available to its packaging network. The pressure on competitors would come less from a dramatic capacity shock and more from improved cost, product mix and service from an integrated producer. ... Qualification and ramp-up proceed steadily, but the economics appear in stages. Full run rate is reached in Q1 2027 and the market gets a clearer view during 2027 of where the new grades are being used and which regional box markets benefit most. ... Qualification takes longer, operating stability is uneven or the final mix does not create the expected value. The $250 million project still operates, but the strategic and financial benefits take longer to show up. ... 1. Capacity disclosure — does International Paper finally provide an annual PM16 containerboard figure? 2. Grade mix — how much detail does the company give on lightweight and high-performance products? 3. Customer qualification — does management move from saying the machine is being qualified to describing meaningful commercial use across product lines? 4. Ramp timing — does Q1 2027 remain the full-run-rate target? 5. Network economics — do future results or management comments show measurable improvements in cost, reliability, freight or box-network performance linked to Riverdale? ... International Paper has spent $250 million and completed the mechanical conversion. Riverdale now has to prove that the new PM16 can make qualified containerboard at the cost, quality and consistency required by the packaging network. The larger strategic picture is already visible: about $550 million of announced investment across two Riverdale machine conversions, more than 750 people at a mill International Paper continues to back, and a corporate strategy built around making the right paper in the right place at a lower cost. For the corrugated board market, the key question is not simply how many tons PM16 can theoretically make. It is how many qualified, competitive tons International Paper can place into its box network — and what happens to regional customers, paper pricing and converter margins when it does.

headline: ITC Completes Century Pulp and Paper Acquisition - Industrial Front
summary_text: ITC Limited has officially completed the integration of Century Pulp and Paper into its Paperboards and Specialty Papers Division (ITC-PSPD), pushing the company’s total paper and paperboard capacity up by more than 50% to approximately 1.5 million metric tonnes. The completion, announced on August 3, 2026, gives ITC its first major manufacturing footprint in northern India for this business and expands its access to key raw materials and customers in the region. ITC’s paperboards division has built its reputation on packaging board, specialty papers and value-added paperboard (VAP) products used across FMCG, pharmaceutical and cigarette packaging. Acquiring Century Pulp and Paper gives ITC-PSPD a strategically located production base in northern India, reducing its dependence on southern and eastern mills and cutting logistics costs for customers based in the north. The deal also expands ITC’s access to wood and pulp raw material sourcing in the Uttarakhand belt at a time when domestic wood prices have stayed elevated and import competition has squeezed margins across the paper sector. With capacity now near 1.5 million metric tonnes, ITC-PSPD strengthens its position against rivals such as JK Paper, West Coast Paper Mills and Emami Paper Mills, all of which have themselves expanded capacity over the past year. ... The completion of the Century Pulp deal comes as the Indian paper industry navigates a mix of pressures: elevated wood costs, competitively priced imports and a government-imposed Minimum Import Price (MIP) of Rs 67,220 per metric tonne on virgin multi-layer paperboard imports that runs until March 31, 2026. Larger, better-integrated players like ITC-PSPD are better placed to absorb these cost pressures than smaller regional mills, and the deal is likely to accelerate consolidation in India’s paperboard segment. It also signals confidence in long-term demand for sustainable, fibre-based packaging as brands shift away from single-use plastics under India’s tightened Extended Producer Responsibility rules. ... ITC shares have traded in a relatively tight band following the announcement, with the paperboards business representing one part of the diversified conglomerate’s broader FMCG, hotels and cigarettes portfolio. Within the paper trade press, the deal has been described as a strategic leap that gives ITC-PSPD a genuine pan-India manufacturing spread for the first time. Competing paper stocks, including JK Paper, Emami Paper Mills and West Coast Paper Mills, have separately rallied in recent sessions on strong quarterly results and import-price-linked pricing power, underscoring an industry-wide environment of consolidation and margin recovery even as individual companies pursue different growth strategies. ... ITC-PSPD is expected to spend the coming quarters integrating Century Pulp and Paper’s operations, including aligning production planning, sourcing and sales channels with its existing mills. Analysts will watch ITC’s upcoming quarterly results for early signs of synergy benefits and utilisation rates at the newly acquired Uttarakhand facility. The broader industry will also be watching whether the Minimum Import Price on paperboard imports is extended beyond its March 2026 deadline, a decision that will materially affect pricing power for ITC-PSPD and its rivals through the rest of the fiscal year. Investors and paper traders are also expected to track how quickly ITC-PSPD ramps up utilisation at the Uttarakhand facility and whether the company announces any further debottlenecking or brownfield expansion at its existing paperboard mills to complement the newly acquired capacity. ... ITC’s total paper and paperboard capacity has grown by more than 50% following the Century Pulp and Paper integration, taking it to approximately 1.5 million metric tonnes. ... headline: IP’s box volumes rise, but external conditions mute demand | Packaging Dive
summary_text: # IP’s box volumes rise, but external conditions mute demand International Paper expects geopolitical and economic conditions to offset some gains from recent price increases. Executives updated progress on the company’s split. Published July 30, 2026 Katie Pyzyk Lead Reporter International Paper’s broke ground on its greenfield box plant in Waterloo, Iowa, in May 2025. It expects startup in Q4 2026 and full production in early 2027. Courtesy of International Paper By the numbers: Q2 2026 Net sales: $6B Down 2.2% year over year EMEA packaging net sales: $2.29B Down 0.2% year over year Net loss: $12M Compared with a $75M net profit in Q2 2025 Even though International Paper had a particularly heavy outage schedule during the second quarter, roughly double typical levels, the company saw improvements in performance, said CEO Andy Silvernail during Thursday’s earnings call. He credited the ongoing work on the company’s optimization plan despite various economic and geopolitical challenges, such as the war with Iran and input cost inflation, mainly for OCC. Per-day box volumes in North America increased 1.7% year over year. Mill performance improved by approximatedly 500 basis points year over year. However, demand was “softer than we had expected” and inflation was significantly higher, Silvernail said, prompting the company to rework its expectations for demand growth in 2026. ... about the cyclosporiasis parasite outbreak ... IP’s plan to split the company into two geographically-oriented businesses is reportedly on track to occur by early next year, as announced in January. Also, as suggested earlier this year, IP has accelerated ongoing cost removal actions in the Europe, Middle East and Africa region ahead of the split. To date, the company has achieved more than $210 million of run-rate savings in EMEA from closing 31 facilities and an office and from reducing headcount in the region by more than 3,000. ... Capital saved from the multitude of facility closures and employee separations during the last 18 months has been reinvested in areas with greater opportunities for returns, Silvernail said. He provided updates on four North American investments: two acquisitions and two facility build-outs. IP completed its acquisition of North Pacific Packaging Co. in June. The facility had impacts from the white liquor implosion disaster at Nippon Dynawave Packaging Co.’s neighboring mill in Longview, Washington, in May, which left 11 people dead and eight others injured. ... Also in Q2, IP completed the acquisition of Delmarva Corrugated Packaging in Delaware. This deal “strengthens our footprint in an attractive region” and supports long-term growth plans,” Silvernail said. The conversion of an uncoated freesheet machine at the Riverdale mill in Selma, Alabama, to produce containerboard is complete, and ramp-up is going according to schedule. ... IP still expects to start up a new greenfield box plant in Waterloo, Iowa, during the fourth quarter with full production slated for Q2 2027. ... Just days before the earnings call, IP announced its third containerboard price increase of 2026, for $80 per ton, to take effect Sept. 1; that follow’s Packaging Corporation of America’s announcement of a $140 per ton increase, widely called unprecedented. IP executives expect that increase to be fully realized by Q1 to Q2 2027. “Obviously we would expect some of it to flow through attractively to the bottom line, but we'll have to see kind of what happens” in the coming months, given challenging external conditions like the war, Silvernail said. Energy and OCC price inflation is expected to offset some of the gains. ... IP anticipates a “step-up” in its North American earnings for the second half of the year. The region’s full-year adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization is $2.35 billion to $2.45 billion, lowering the top range by about $50 million, executives said. “There’s a lot of uncertainty out there with what’s happening in the Middle East,” Silvernail said, in addition to other factors including inflation, so IP now does not expect demand to increase notably in the second half of 2026. It now expects relatively flat demand in North America and a modest uptick in Europe. “And we’ll see what that means for ‘27,” he said.

headline: International Paper to Shutter Four North American Plants as Network Overhaul Accelerates - Industrial Front
summary_text: International Paper has announced plans to cease preprint operations at its Richwood, Kentucky facility and close its Aurora, Illinois sheet plant along with converting plants in Elk Grove, California and Barrington, New Jersey by the end of the third quarter of 2026. The closures mark one of the most significant network restructuring moves by a major North American paper producer this year, reflecting a broader industry push to consolidate capacity around fewer, more efficient facilities. ... The company has described the closures as part of a wider transformation of its North America packaging network, aimed at concentrating production in facilities with higher automation, lower per-unit energy costs, and better proximity to key e-commerce and consumer goods customers. Rather than a simple cost-cutting exercise, the restructuring reflects a recognition that legacy converting and preprint operations built for an earlier era of retail packaging demand no longer align with today’s containerboard and corrugated packaging growth patterns, which are increasingly concentrated around fulfillment centers and regional distribution hubs. ... International Paper’s move fits a broader pattern across the pulp and paper sector, where packaging grades including cartonboard, containerboard, and kraft papers are expected to sustain positive performance fueled by persistent e-commerce demand and continued plastic substitution, even as graphic and specialty paper segments face structural decline. Companies across the industry are responding by shifting capital and operational focus toward packaging grades while shuttering or repurposing capacity tied to printing and legacy paper products experiencing secular demand erosion. ... The closures will affect production workers across four states, with the companies expected to offer severance packages and, in some cases, transfer opportunities to nearby facilities as part of standard practice for planned plant closures of this scale. Local officials in the affected communities, particularly Aurora and Richwood, are likely to face the broader economic ripple effects that accompany large industrial facility closures, from reduced local tax revenue to knock-on effects for regional suppliers and logistics providers. ... Even as certain facility types close, the broader fiber-based packaging opportunity remains a central growth thesis for the sector. Fibre-based food packaging is on course to become the leading sustainable packaging material by 2045, driven by breakthrough barrier coating technologies that allow paper-based packaging to replace plastic in food contact applications, alongside tightening global regulation favoring recyclable and biodegradable materials over conventional plastics. ... Analysts covering the company will be watching how quickly International Paper redirects capital freed by the closures toward higher-growth packaging capacity, and whether the network consolidation improves margins enough to offset near-term restructuring charges. The move is likely to be viewed as a template for how legacy North American paper producers are choosing to navigate a market increasingly bifurcated between declining print-paper demand and robust, e-commerce-driven packaging growth.

headline: Arbex debuts with R$18bn in revenue as Suzano expands tissue business
summary_text: Arbex debuts with R$18bn in revenue as Suzano expands tissue business ... over three years ... 07 ... 07h3 ... Created by Suzano and U.S.-based Kimberly-Clark, Arbex debuts as one of the world's largest tissue paper companies. The joint venture, completed on Wednesday (1) and valued at $3.7 billion (R$19.2 billion at current exchange rates), launches with annual revenue of $3.5 billion (R$18.1 billion) and aims to become the most efficient integrated tissue company in the global industry. Suzano, which announced a year ago the acquisition of a 51% stake in Kimberly-Clark’s global tissue operations outside the U.S., holds a controlling stake in the new company. Kimberly-Clark owns the remaining 49%. “Our ambition is not to be the largest company in the sector, but the most efficient,” Suzano CEO Beto Abreu told Valor. Arbex’s initial business plan is centered on that goal, prioritizing cost reductions to improve efficiency over the short and medium term. “We have publicly committed to generating $175 million in operational efficiencies over the next three years. Before thinking about the next stage of growth, we need to deliver on that commitment. We need to earn the right to grow, and that is our objective in the short and medium term,” he said. At the same time, the transaction strengthens Suzano’s strategy to expand pulp sales. As part of its strategy to replace softwood pulp with hardwood pulp, Suzano plans to accelerate Arbex’s adoption of hardwood fiber, where the Brazilian company holds a competitive edge. “We will accelerate that process within Arbex,” Abreu said. Suzano had already been the exclusive supplier of hardwood pulp to all Kimberly-Clark operations. Under the new structure, it will remain the exclusive supplier indefinitely for the businesses now housed within Arbex. “When manufacturing products such as paper towels and toilet paper, you can use anywhere from 70% to 100% hardwood pulp, with the remainder being softwood. That transition will now accelerate because we operate the machines that previously belonged to Kimberly-Clark’s international business,” Abreu explained. Arbex now encompasses Kimberly-Clark’s production and sales of products such as toilet paper, napkins, paper towels, and facial tissues outside the United States. The transaction also transfers 22 manufacturing facilities across 14 countries in Europe, Asia, the Middle East, South America, Central America, Africa, and Oceania to the new company. ... Suzano formally assumed control of the new company on Wednesday (1) after paying $1.3 billion for its 51% stake. By announcing the transaction, the partners disclosed that Suzano would have the option to acquire the remaining 49% at any time, using the same valuation multiple—6.5 times earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA)—that determined the original purchase price. According to Abreu, however, Suzano has no intention of exercising that option in the short or medium term. “We like the partnership because our capabilities are complementary. We bring industrial operating expertise, while they contribute brand strength and product development,” he said. Abreu said the efficiency gains outlined in Arbex’s business plan will come primarily from lower manufacturing and administrative costs, the development of regional suppliers, and supply chain optimization. “We have many tools and technologies that can generate significant gains in logistics throughout the supply chain and distribution process from Arbex’s plants to customers in 70 countries,” he said. For Suzano, Kimberly-Clark’s decision to divest part of its international operations reflects its confidence that the Brazilian company can unlock greater value from those assets. “I imagine they believe the company will generate ... value under our management than it would under theirs alone, because a global multinational does not always have the same speed to advance certain strategic initiatives,” Abreu said. The new company’s leadership combines executives from both partners. Ehab Abou-Oaf, who already headed the international operations now integrated into Arbex, remains CEO. Luís Bueno, formerly Suzano’s executive vice president for consumer goods, becomes chief operating officer, while Oscar Mousinho, formerly chief financial officer of Mars’s animal nutrition business, assumes the CFO role. “We have the prerogative to appoint the CEO and CFO, but we chose to recommend the current CEO because of his experience and brought in a CFO from outside the company,” Abreu said. According to Abreu, Arbex will operate independently from both Suzano and Kimberly-Clark. Its financial results, however, will be fully consolidated into Suzano’s financial statements and reported separately from the tissue business Suzano already operates in Brazil. ... possibility of further acquisitions, Abreu said the company’s current priority is “deleveraging and generating value from investments already made before considering new moves.” He added that the $1.3 billion cash payment is not expected to increase Suzano’s leverage materially. Citi analysts said the creation of Arbex marks a milestone for Suzano given the size of the investment. They said investors are now likely to focus on the company’s ability to rebuild cash generation and expect Arbex’s operating volumes to begin being consolidated into Suzano’s results starting in the third quarter. On the day Arbex was launched, Suzano’s shares rose 2.1%, the second-best performance on the Ibovespa, closing at R$40.59. The stock, however, remains down 21.1% so far this year, according to Valor Data. (Adriana Peraita contributed reporting)
